        - generic [ref=f84e635]:

        - heading [level=1] [ref=f84e638]:
          - text: Struct Vec
          - button "Copy item path" [ref=f84e639] [cursor=pointer]
        - generic [ref=f84e640]:
          - link "Write" [ref=f84e642] [cursor=pointer]:

          - text: Since 1.0.0 ·
          - link "Source" [ref=f84e643] [cursor=pointer]:

        - generic [ref=f84e644]:
          - link "Search" [ref=f84e646] [cursor=pointer]:

          - link "Settings" [ref=f84e649] [cursor=pointer]:

      - code [ref=f84e657]:
        - text: pub struct Vec<T, A =
        - link "Global" [ref=f84e658] [cursor=pointer]:
          - /url: ../alloc/struct.Global.html
        - text: ">"
        - generic [ref=f84e659]:
          - text: "where A:"
          - link "Allocator" [ref=f84e660] [cursor=pointer]:
            - /url: ../alloc/trait.Allocator.html

      - group [ref=f84e661]:
        - generic "Collapse" [ref=f84e662] [cursor=pointer]
        - generic [ref=f84e663]:
          - paragraph [ref=f84e664]:
            - text: A contiguous growable array type, written as
            - code [ref=f84e665]: Vec<T>
            - text: ", short for ‘vector’."
          - heading "Examples" [level=2] [ref=f84e666]
          - code [ref=f84e669]: "let mut vec = Vec::new(); vec.push(1); vec.push(2); assert_eq!(vec.len(), 2); assert_eq!(vec[0], 1); assert_eq!(vec.pop(), Some(2)); assert_eq!(vec.len(), 1); vec[0] = 7; assert_eq!(vec[0], 7); vec.extend([1, 2, 3]); for x in &vec { println!(\"{x}\"); } assert_eq!(vec, [7, 1, 2, 3]);"
          - paragraph [ref=f84e670]:
            - text: The
            - link [ref=f84e671] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../macro.vec.html
              - code [ref=f84e672]: vec!
            - text: "macro is provided for convenient initialization:"
          - code [ref=f84e675]: let mut vec1 = vec![1, 2, 3]; vec1.push(4); let vec2 = Vec::from([1, 2, 3, 4]); assert_eq!(vec1, vec2);
          - paragraph [ref=f84e676]:
            - text: It can also initialize each element of a
            - code [ref=f84e677]: Vec<T>
            - text: "with a given value. This may be more efficient than performing allocation and initialization in separate steps, especially when initializing a vector of zeros:"
          - code [ref=f84e680]: "let vec = vec![0; 5]; assert_eq!(vec, [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]); // The following is equivalent, but potentially slower: let mut vec = Vec::with_capacity(5); vec.resize(5, 0); assert_eq!(vec, [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]);"
          - paragraph [ref=f84e681]:
            - text: For more information, see
            - link "Capacity and Reallocation" [ref=f84e682] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: "#capacity-and-reallocation"
            - text: .
          - paragraph [ref=f84e683]:
            - text: Use a
            - code [ref=f84e684]: Vec<T>
            - text: "as an efficient stack:"
          - code [ref=f84e687]: "let mut stack = Vec::new(); stack.push(1); stack.push(2); stack.push(3); while let Some(top) = stack.pop() { // Prints 3, 2, 1 println!(\"{top}\"); }"
          - heading "Indexing" [level=2] [ref=f84e688]
          - paragraph [ref=f84e689]:
            - text: The
            - code [ref=f84e690]: Vec
            - text: type allows access to values by index, because it implements the
            - link [ref=f84e691] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../ops/trait.Index.html
              - code [ref=f84e692]: Index
            - text: "trait. An example will be more explicit:"
          - code [ref=f84e695]: "let v = vec![0, 2, 4, 6]; println!(\"{}\", v[1]); // it will display '2'"
          - paragraph [ref=f84e696]:
            - text: "However be careful: if you try to access an index which isn’t in the"
            - code [ref=f84e697]: Vec
            - text: ", your software will panic! You cannot do this:"
          - generic [ref=f84e698]:
            - link "ⓘ" [ref=f84e699] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: "#"
            - code [ref=f84e701]: "let v = vec![0, 2, 4, 6]; println!(\"{}\", v[6]); // it will panic!"
          - paragraph [ref=f84e702]:
            - text: Use
            - link [ref=f84e703] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../primitive.slice.html#method.get
              - code [ref=f84e704]: get
            - text: and
            - link [ref=f84e705] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../primitive.slice.html#method.get_mut
              - code [ref=f84e706]: get_mut
            - text: if you want to check whether the index is in the
            - code [ref=f84e707]: Vec
            - text: .
          - heading "Slicing" [level=2] [ref=f84e708]
          - paragraph [ref=f84e709]:
            - text: A
            - code [ref=f84e710]: Vec
            - text: can be mutable. On the other hand, slices are read-only objects. To get a
            - link "slice" [ref=f84e711] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../primitive.slice.html
            - text: ", use"
            - link [ref=f84e712] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../primitive.reference.html
              - code [ref=f84e713]: "&"
            - text: ". Example:"
          - code [ref=f84e716]: "fn read_slice(slice: &[usize]) { // ... } let v = vec![0, 1]; read_slice(&v); // ... and that's all! // you can also do it like this: let u: &[usize] = &v; // or like this: let u: &[_] = &v;"
          - paragraph [ref=f84e717]:
            - text: In Rust, it’s more common to pass slices as arguments rather than vectors when you just want to provide read access. The same goes for
            - link [ref=f84e718] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../string/struct.String.html
              - code [ref=f84e719]: String
            - text: and
            - link [ref=f84e720] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../primitive.str.html
              - code [ref=f84e721]: "&str"
            - text: .
          - heading "Capacity and reallocation" [level=2] [ref=f84e722]
          - paragraph [ref=f84e723]:
            - text: The capacity of a vector is the amount of space allocated for any future elements that will be added onto the vector. This is not to be confused with the
            - emphasis [ref=f84e724]: length
            - text: of a vector, which specifies the number of actual elements within the vector. If a vector’s length exceeds its capacity, its capacity will automatically be increased, but its elements will have to be reallocated.
          - paragraph [ref=f84e725]:
            - text: For example, a vector with capacity 10 and length 0 would be an empty vector with space for 10 more elements. Pushing 10 or fewer elements onto the vector will not change its capacity or cause reallocation to occur. However, if the vector’s length is increased to 11, it will have to reallocate, which can be slow. For this reason, it is recommended to use
            - link [ref=f84e726] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.with_capacity
              - code [ref=f84e727]: Vec::with_capacity
            - text: whenever possible to specify how big the vector is expected to get.
          - heading "Guarantees" [level=2] [ref=f84e728]
          - paragraph [ref=f84e729]:
            - text: Due to its incredibly fundamental nature,
            - code [ref=f84e730]: Vec
            - text: makes a lot of guarantees about its design. This ensures that it’s as low-overhead as possible in the general case, and can be correctly manipulated in primitive ways by unsafe code. Note that these guarantees refer to an unqualified
            - code [ref=f84e731]: Vec<T>
            - text: . If additional type parameters are added (e.g., to support custom allocators), overriding their defaults may change the behavior.
          - paragraph [ref=f84e732]:
            - text: Most fundamentally,
            - code [ref=f84e733]: Vec
            - text: is and always will be a (pointer, capacity, length) triplet. No more, no less. The order of these fields is completely unspecified, and you should use the appropriate methods to modify these. The pointer will never be null, so this type is null-pointer-optimized.
          - paragraph [ref=f84e734]:
            - text: However, the pointer might not actually point to allocated memory. In particular, if you construct a
            - code [ref=f84e735]: Vec
            - text: with capacity 0 via
            - link [ref=f84e736] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.new
              - code [ref=f84e737]: Vec::new
            - text: ","
            - link [ref=f84e738] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../macro.vec.html
              - code [ref=f84e739]: vec![]
            - text: ","
            - link [ref=f84e740] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.with_capacity
              - code [ref=f84e741]: Vec::with_capacity(0)
            - text: ", or by calling"
            - link [ref=f84e742] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.shrink_to_fit
              - code [ref=f84e743]: shrink_to_fit
            - text: on an empty Vec, it will not allocate memory. Similarly, if you store zero-sized types inside a
            - code [ref=f84e744]: Vec
            - text: ", it will not allocate space for them."
            - emphasis [ref=f84e745]:
              - text: Note that in this case the
              - code [ref=f84e746]: Vec
              - text: might not report a
              - link [ref=f84e747] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.capacity
                - code [ref=f84e748]: capacity
              - text: of 0
            - text: .
            - code [ref=f84e749]: Vec
            - text: will allocate if and only if
            - code [ref=f84e750]:
              - link "size_of::<T>" [ref=f84e751] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: ../mem/fn.size_of.html
              - text: () *
              - link "capacity" [ref=f84e752] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.capacity
              - text: () > 0
            - text: . In general,
            - code [ref=f84e753]: Vec
            - text: ’s allocation details are very subtle — if you intend to allocate memory using a
            - code [ref=f84e754]: Vec
            - text: and use it for something else (either to pass to unsafe code, or to build your own memory-backed collection), be sure to deallocate this memory by using
            - code [ref=f84e755]: from_raw_parts
            - text: to recover the
            - code [ref=f84e756]: Vec
            - text: and then dropping it.
          - paragraph [ref=f84e757]:
            - text: If a
            - code [ref=f84e758]: Vec
            - emphasis [ref=f84e759]: has
            - text: allocated memory, then the memory it points to is on the heap (as defined by the allocator Rust is configured to use by default), and its pointer points to
            - link [ref=f84e760] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.len
              - code [ref=f84e761]: len
            - text: initialized, contiguous elements in order (what you would see if you coerced it to a slice), followed by
            - code [ref=f84e762]:
              - link "capacity" [ref=f84e763] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.capacity
              - text: "-"
              - link "len" [ref=f84e764] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.len
            - text: logically uninitialized, contiguous elements.
          - paragraph [ref=f84e765]:
            - text: A vector containing the elements
            - code [ref=f84e766]: "'a'"
            - text: and
            - code [ref=f84e767]: "'b'"
            - text: with capacity 4 can be visualized as below. The top part is the
            - code [ref=f84e768]: Vec
            - text: struct, it contains a pointer to the head of the allocation in the heap, length and capacity. The bottom part is the allocation on the heap, a contiguous memory block.
          - code [ref=f84e771]: ptr len capacity +--------+--------+--------+ | 0x0123 | 2 | 4 | +--------+--------+--------+ | v Heap +--------+--------+--------+--------+ | 'a' | 'b' | uninit | uninit | +--------+--------+--------+--------+
          - list [ref=f84e772]:
            - listitem [ref=f84e773]:
              - strong [ref=f84e774]: uninit
              - text: represents memory that is not initialized, see
              - link [ref=f84e775] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: ../mem/union.MaybeUninit.html
                - code [ref=f84e776]: MaybeUninit
              - text: .
            - listitem [ref=f84e777]:
              - text: "Note: the ABI is not stable and"
              - code [ref=f84e778]: Vec
              - text: makes no guarantees about its memory layout (including the order of fields).
          - paragraph [ref=f84e779]:
            - code [ref=f84e780]: Vec
            - text: "will never perform a “small optimization” where elements are actually stored on the stack for two reasons:"
          - list [ref=f84e781]:
            - listitem [ref=f84e782]:
              - paragraph [ref=f84e783]:
                - text: It would make it more difficult for unsafe code to correctly manipulate a
                - code [ref=f84e784]: Vec
                - text: . The contents of a
                - code [ref=f84e785]: Vec
                - text: wouldn’t have a stable address if it were only moved, and it would be more difficult to determine if a
                - code [ref=f84e786]: Vec
                - text: had actually allocated memory.
            - listitem [ref=f84e787]:
              - paragraph [ref=f84e788]: It would penalize the general case, incurring an additional branch on every access.
          - paragraph [ref=f84e789]:
            - code [ref=f84e790]: Vec
            - text: will never automatically shrink itself, even if completely empty. This ensures no unnecessary allocations or deallocations occur. Emptying a
            - code [ref=f84e791]: Vec
            - text: and then filling it back up to the same
            - link [ref=f84e792] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.len
              - code [ref=f84e793]: len
            - text: should incur no calls to the allocator. If you wish to free up unused memory, use
            - link [ref=f84e794] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.shrink_to_fit
              - code [ref=f84e795]: shrink_to_fit
            - text: or
            - link [ref=f84e796] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.shrink_to
              - code [ref=f84e797]: shrink_to
            - text: .
          - paragraph [ref=f84e798]:
            - link [ref=f84e799] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.push
              - code [ref=f84e800]: push
            - text: and
            - link [ref=f84e801] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.insert
              - code [ref=f84e802]: insert
            - text: will never (re)allocate if the reported capacity is sufficient.
            - link [ref=f84e803] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.push
              - code [ref=f84e804]: push
            - text: and
            - link [ref=f84e805] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.insert
              - code [ref=f84e806]: insert
            - emphasis [ref=f84e807]: will
            - text: (re)allocate if
            - code [ref=f84e808]:
              - link "len" [ref=f84e809] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.len
              - text: ==
              - link "capacity" [ref=f84e810] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.capacity
            - text: . That is, the reported capacity is completely accurate, and can be relied on. It can even be used to manually free the memory allocated by a
            - code [ref=f84e811]: Vec
            - text: if desired. Bulk insertion methods
            - emphasis [ref=f84e812]: may
            - text: reallocate, even when not necessary.
          - paragraph [ref=f84e813]:
            - code [ref=f84e814]: Vec
            - text: does not guarantee any particular growth strategy when reallocating when full, nor when
            - link [ref=f84e815] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.reserve
              - code [ref=f84e816]: reserve
            - text: is called. The current strategy is basic and it may prove desirable to use a non-constant growth factor. Whatever strategy is used will of course guarantee
            - emphasis [ref=f84e817]: O
            - text: (1) amortized
            - link [ref=f84e818] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.push
              - code [ref=f84e819]: push
            - text: .
          - paragraph [ref=f84e820]:
            - text: It is guaranteed, in order to respect the intentions of the programmer, that all of
            - code [ref=f84e821]: vec![e_1, e_2, ..., e_n]
            - text: ","
            - code [ref=f84e822]: vec![x; n]
            - text: ", and"
            - link [ref=f84e823] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.with_capacity
              - code [ref=f84e824]: Vec::with_capacity(n)
            - text: produce a
            - code [ref=f84e825]: Vec
            - text: that requests an allocation of the exact size needed for precisely
            - code [ref=f84e826]: "n"
            - text: "elements from the allocator, and no other size (such as, for example: a size rounded up to the nearest power of 2). The allocator will return an allocation that is at least as large as requested, but it may be larger."
          - paragraph [ref=f84e827]:
            - text: It is guaranteed that the
            - link [ref=f84e828] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.capacity
              - code [ref=f84e829]: Vec::capacity
            - text: method returns a value that is at least the requested capacity and not more than the allocated capacity.
          - paragraph [ref=f84e830]:
            - text: The method
            - link [ref=f84e831] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.shrink_to_fit
              - code [ref=f84e832]: Vec::shrink_to_fit
            - text: will attempt to discard excess capacity an allocator has given to a
            - code [ref=f84e833]: Vec
            - text: . If
            - code [ref=f84e834]:
              - link "len" [ref=f84e835] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.len
              - text: ==
              - link "capacity" [ref=f84e836] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.capacity
            - text: ", then a"
            - code [ref=f84e837]: Vec<T>
            - text: can be converted to and from a
            - link [ref=f84e838] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: ../boxed/struct.Box.html
              - code [ref=f84e839]: Box<[T]>
            - text: without reallocating or moving the elements.
            - code [ref=f84e840]: Vec
            - text: exploits this fact as much as reasonable when implementing common conversions such as
            - link [ref=f84e841] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.into_boxed_slice
              - code [ref=f84e842]: into_boxed_slice
            - text: .
          - paragraph [ref=f84e843]:
            - code [ref=f84e844]: Vec
            - text: will not specifically overwrite any data that is removed from it, but also won’t specifically preserve it. Its uninitialized memory is scratch space that it may use however it wants. It will generally just do whatever is most efficient or otherwise easy to implement. Do not rely on removed data to be erased for security purposes. Even if you drop a
            - code [ref=f84e845]: Vec
            - text: ", its buffer may simply be reused by another allocation. Even if you zero a"
            - code [ref=f84e846]: Vec
            - text: "’s memory first, that might not actually happen because the optimizer does not consider this a side-effect that must be preserved. There is one case which we will not break, however: using"
            - code [ref=f84e847]: unsafe
            - text: code to write to the excess capacity, and then increasing the length to match, is always valid.
          - paragraph [ref=f84e848]:
            - text: Currently,
            - code [ref=f84e849]: Vec
            - text: does not guarantee the order in which elements are dropped. The order has changed in the past and may change again.
      - heading "Implementations" [level=2] [ref=f84e850]

                  - heading [level=4] [ref=f84e882]:
                    - text: pub fn
                    - link "with_capacity" [ref=f84e883] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#method.with_capacity"
                    - text: "(capacity:"
                    - link "usize" [ref=f84e884] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../primitive.usize.html

                    - link "Vec" [ref=f84e885] [cursor=pointer]:

              - generic [ref=f84e886]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e887]:
                  - text: Constructs a new, empty
                  - code [ref=f84e888]: Vec<T>
                  - text: with at least the specified capacity.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e889]:
                  - text: The vector will be able to hold at least
                  - code [ref=f84e890]: capacity
                  - text: elements without reallocating. This method is allowed to allocate for more elements than
                  - code [ref=f84e891]: capacity
                  - text: . If
                  - code [ref=f84e892]: capacity
                  - text: is zero, the vector will not allocate.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e893]:
                  - text: It is important to note that although the returned vector has the minimum
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e894]: capacity
                  - text: specified, the vector will have a zero
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e895]: length
                  - text: . For an explanation of the difference between length and capacity, see
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e896]:
                    - link "Capacity and reallocation" [ref=f84e897] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#capacity-and-reallocation"
                  - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e898]:
                  - text: If it is important to know the exact allocated capacity of a
                  - code [ref=f84e899]: Vec
                  - text: ", always use the"
                  - link [ref=f84e900] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.capacity
                    - code [ref=f84e901]: capacity
                  - text: method after construction.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e902]:
                  - text: For
                  - code [ref=f84e903]: Vec<T>
                  - text: where
                  - code [ref=f84e904]: T
                  - text: is a zero-sized type, there will be no allocation and the capacity will always be
                  - code [ref=f84e905]: usize::MAX
                  - text: .
                - heading "Panics" [level=5] [ref=f84e906]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e907]:
                  - text: Panics if the new capacity exceeds
                  - code [ref=f84e908]: isize::MAX
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e909]: bytes
                  - text: .
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e910]
                - code [ref=f84e913]: "let mut vec = Vec::with_capacity(10); // The vector contains no items, even though it has capacity for more assert_eq!(vec.len(), 0); assert!(vec.capacity() >= 10); // These are all done without reallocating... for i in 0..10 { vec.push(i); } assert_eq!(vec.len(), 10); assert!(vec.capacity() >= 10); // ...but this may make the vector reallocate vec.push(11); assert_eq!(vec.len(), 11); assert!(vec.capacity() >= 11); // A vector of a zero-sized type will always over-allocate, since no // allocation is necessary let vec_units = Vec::<()>::with_capacity(10); assert_eq!(vec_units.capacity(), usize::MAX);"
            - group [ref=f84e914]:

                  - heading [level=4] [ref=f84e947]:
                    - text: pub unsafe fn
                    - link "from_raw_parts" [ref=f84e948] [cursor=pointer]:

              - generic [ref=f84e953]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e954]:
                  - text: Creates a
                  - code [ref=f84e955]: Vec<T>
                  - text: directly from a pointer, a length, and a capacity.
                - heading "Safety" [level=5] [ref=f84e956]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e957]: "This is highly unsafe, due to the number of invariants that aren’t checked:"
                - list [ref=f84e958]:
                  - listitem [ref=f84e959]:
                    - text: If
                    - code [ref=f84e960]: T
                    - text: is not a zero-sized type and the capacity is nonzero,
                    - code [ref=f84e961]: ptr
                    - text: must have been allocated using the global allocator, such as via the
                    - link [ref=f84e962] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../alloc/fn.alloc.html
                      - code [ref=f84e963]: alloc::alloc
                    - text: function. If
                    - code [ref=f84e964]: T
                    - text: is a zero-sized type or the capacity is zero,
                    - code [ref=f84e965]: ptr
                    - text: need only be non-null and aligned.
                  - listitem [ref=f84e966]:
                    - code [ref=f84e967]: T
                    - text: needs to have the same alignment as what
                    - code [ref=f84e968]: ptr
                    - text: was allocated with, if the pointer is required to be allocated. (
                    - code [ref=f84e969]: T
                    - text: having a less strict alignment is not sufficient, the alignment really needs to be equal to satisfy the
                    - link [ref=f84e970] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#tymethod.dealloc
                      - code [ref=f84e971]: dealloc
                    - text: requirement that memory must be allocated and deallocated with the same layout.)
                  - listitem [ref=f84e972]:
                    - text: The size of
                    - code [ref=f84e973]: T
                    - text: times the
                    - code [ref=f84e974]: capacity
                    - text: (i.e. the allocated size in bytes), if nonzero, needs to be the same size as the pointer was allocated with. (Because similar to alignment,
                    - link [ref=f84e975] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#tymethod.dealloc
                      - code [ref=f84e976]: dealloc
                    - text: must be called with the same layout
                    - code [ref=f84e977]: size
                    - text: .)
                  - listitem [ref=f84e978]:
                    - code [ref=f84e979]: length
                    - text: needs to be less than or equal to
                    - code [ref=f84e980]: capacity
                    - text: .
                  - listitem [ref=f84e981]:
                    - text: The first
                    - code [ref=f84e982]: length
                    - text: values must be properly initialized values of type
                    - code [ref=f84e983]: T
                    - text: .
                  - listitem [ref=f84e984]:
                    - code [ref=f84e985]: capacity
                    - text: needs to be the capacity that the pointer was allocated with, if the pointer is required to be allocated.
                  - listitem [ref=f84e986]:
                    - text: The allocated size in bytes must be no larger than
                    - code [ref=f84e987]: isize::MAX
                    - text: . See the safety documentation of
                    - link [ref=f84e988] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../primitive.pointer.html#method.offset
                      - code [ref=f84e989]: pointer::offset
                    - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e990]:
                  - text: These requirements are always upheld by any
                  - code [ref=f84e991]: ptr
                  - text: that has been allocated via
                  - code [ref=f84e992]: Vec<T>
                  - text: . Other allocation sources are allowed if the invariants are upheld.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e993]:
                  - text: Violating these may cause problems like corrupting the allocator’s internal data structures. For example it is normally
                  - strong [ref=f84e994]: not
                  - text: safe to build a
                  - code [ref=f84e995]: Vec<u8>
                  - text: from a pointer to a C
                  - code [ref=f84e996]: char
                  - text: array with length
                  - code [ref=f84e997]: size_t
                  - text: ", doing so is only safe if the array was initially allocated by a"
                  - code [ref=f84e998]: Vec
                  - text: or
                  - code [ref=f84e999]: String
                  - text: . It’s also not safe to build one from a
                  - code [ref=f84e1000]: Vec<u16>
                  - text: and its length, because the allocator cares about the alignment, and these two types have different alignments. The buffer was allocated with alignment 2 (for
                  - code [ref=f84e1001]: u16
                  - text: ), but after turning it into a
                  - code [ref=f84e1002]: Vec<u8>
                  - text: it’ll be deallocated with alignment 1. To avoid these issues, it is often preferable to do casting/transmuting using
                  - link [ref=f84e1003] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../slice/fn.from_raw_parts.html
                    - code [ref=f84e1004]: slice::from_raw_parts
                  - text: instead.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1005]:
                  - text: The ownership of
                  - code [ref=f84e1006]: ptr
                  - text: is effectively transferred to the
                  - code [ref=f84e1007]: Vec<T>
                  - text: which may then deallocate, reallocate or change the contents of memory pointed to by the pointer at will. Ensure that nothing else uses the pointer after calling this function.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e1008]
                - code [ref=f84e1011]: "use std::ptr; let v = vec![1, 2, 3]; // Deconstruct the vector into parts. let (p, len, cap) = v.into_raw_parts(); unsafe { // Overwrite memory with 4, 5, 6 for i in 0..len { ptr::write(p.add(i), 4 + i); } // Put everything back together into a Vec let rebuilt = Vec::from_raw_parts(p, len, cap); assert_eq!(rebuilt, [4, 5, 6]); }"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1012]: "Using memory that was allocated elsewhere:"
                - code [ref=f84e1015]: "use std::alloc::{alloc, Layout}; fn main() { let layout = Layout::array::<u32>(16).expect(\"overflow cannot happen\"); let vec = unsafe { let mem = alloc(layout).cast::<u32>(); if mem.is_null() { return; } mem.write(1_000_000); Vec::from_raw_parts(mem, 1, 16) }; assert_eq!(vec, &[1_000_000]); assert_eq!(vec.capacity(), 16); }"

              - generic [ref=f84e1106]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1107]:
                  - text: Creates a
                  - code [ref=f84e1108]: Vec<T>
                  - text: where each element is produced by calling
                  - code [ref=f84e1109]: f
                  - text: with that element’s index while walking forward through the
                  - code [ref=f84e1110]: Vec<T>
                  - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1111]: This is essentially the same as writing
                - code [ref=f84e1114]: vec![f(0), f(1), f(2), …, f(length - 2), f(length - 1)]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1115]:
                  - text: and is similar to
                  - code [ref=f84e1116]: (0..i).map(f)
                  - text: ", just for"
                  - code [ref=f84e1117]: Vec<T>
                  - text: s not iterators.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1118]:
                  - text: If
                  - code [ref=f84e1119]: length == 0
                  - text: ", this produces an empty"
                  - code [ref=f84e1120]: Vec<T>
                  - text: without ever calling
                  - code [ref=f84e1121]: f
                  - text: .
                - heading "Example" [level=5] [ref=f84e1122]
                - code [ref=f84e1125]: "#![feature(vec_from_fn)] let vec = Vec::from_fn(5, |i| i); // indexes are: 0 1 2 3 4 assert_eq!(vec, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]); let vec2 = Vec::from_fn(8, |i| i * 2); // indexes are: 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 assert_eq!(vec2, [0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14]); let bool_vec = Vec::from_fn(5, |i| i % 2 == 0); // indexes are: 0 1 2 3 4 assert_eq!(bool_vec, [true, false, true, false, true]);"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1126]:
                  - text: The
                  - code [ref=f84e1127]: Vec<T>
                  - text: "is generated in ascending index order, starting from the front and going towards the back, so you can use closures with mutable state:"
                - code [ref=f84e1130]: "#![feature(vec_from_fn)] let mut state = 1; let a = Vec::from_fn(6, |_| { let x = state; state *= 2; x }); assert_eq!(a, [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32]);"

              - generic [ref=f84e1143]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1144]:
                  - text: Decomposes a
                  - code [ref=f84e1145]: Vec<T>
                  - text: "into its raw components:"
                  - code [ref=f84e1146]: (pointer, length, capacity)
                  - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1147]:
                  - text: Returns the raw pointer to the underlying data, the length of the vector (in elements), and the allocated capacity of the data (in elements). These are the same arguments in the same order as the arguments to
                  - link [ref=f84e1148] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.from_raw_parts
                    - code [ref=f84e1149]: from_raw_parts
                  - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1150]:
                  - text: After calling this function, the caller is responsible for the memory previously managed by the
                  - code [ref=f84e1151]: Vec
                  - text: . Most often, one does this by converting the raw pointer, length, and capacity back into a
                  - code [ref=f84e1152]: Vec
                  - text: with the
                  - link [ref=f84e1153] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.from_raw_parts
                    - code [ref=f84e1154]: from_raw_parts
                  - text: function; more generally, if
                  - code [ref=f84e1155]: T
                  - text: is non-zero-sized and the capacity is nonzero, one may use any method that calls
                  - link [ref=f84e1156] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#tymethod.dealloc
                    - code [ref=f84e1157]: dealloc
                  - text: with a layout of
                  - code [ref=f84e1158]: Layout::array::<T>(capacity)
                  - text: ; if
                  - code [ref=f84e1159]: T
                  - text: is zero-sized or the capacity is zero, nothing needs to be done.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e1160]
                - code [ref=f84e1163]: "let v: Vec<i32> = vec![-1, 0, 1]; let (ptr, len, cap) = v.into_raw_parts(); let rebuilt = unsafe { // We can now make changes to the components, such as // transmuting the raw pointer to a compatible type. let ptr = ptr as *mut u32; Vec::from_raw_parts(ptr, len, cap) }; assert_eq!(rebuilt, [4294967295, 0, 1]);"

              - generic [ref=f84e1235]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1236]:
                  - text: Constructs a new, empty
                  - code [ref=f84e1237]: Vec<T, A>
                  - text: with at least the specified capacity with the provided allocator.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1238]:
                  - text: The vector will be able to hold at least
                  - code [ref=f84e1239]: capacity
                  - text: elements without reallocating. This method is allowed to allocate for more elements than
                  - code [ref=f84e1240]: capacity
                  - text: . If
                  - code [ref=f84e1241]: capacity
                  - text: is zero, the vector will not allocate.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1242]:
                  - text: It is important to note that although the returned vector has the minimum
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1243]: capacity
                  - text: specified, the vector will have a zero
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1244]: length
                  - text: . For an explanation of the difference between length and capacity, see
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1245]:
                    - link "Capacity and reallocation" [ref=f84e1246] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#capacity-and-reallocation"
                  - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1247]:
                  - text: If it is important to know the exact allocated capacity of a
                  - code [ref=f84e1248]: Vec
                  - text: ", always use the"
                  - link [ref=f84e1249] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.capacity
                    - code [ref=f84e1250]: capacity
                  - text: method after construction.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1251]:
                  - text: For
                  - code [ref=f84e1252]: Vec<T, A>
                  - text: where
                  - code [ref=f84e1253]: T
                  - text: is a zero-sized type, there will be no allocation and the capacity will always be
                  - code [ref=f84e1254]: usize::MAX
                  - text: .
                - heading "Panics" [level=5] [ref=f84e1255]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1256]:
                  - text: Panics if the new capacity exceeds
                  - code [ref=f84e1257]: isize::MAX
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1258]: bytes
                  - text: .
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e1259]
                - code [ref=f84e1262]: "#![feature(allocator_api)] use std::alloc::System; let mut vec = Vec::with_capacity_in(10, System); // The vector contains no items, even though it has capacity for more assert_eq!(vec.len(), 0); assert!(vec.capacity() >= 10); // These are all done without reallocating... for i in 0..10 { vec.push(i); } assert_eq!(vec.len(), 10); assert!(vec.capacity() >= 10); // ...but this may make the vector reallocate vec.push(11); assert_eq!(vec.len(), 11); assert!(vec.capacity() >= 11); // A vector of a zero-sized type will always over-allocate, since no // allocation is necessary let vec_units = Vec::<(), System>::with_capacity_in(10, System); assert_eq!(vec_units.capacity(), usize::MAX);"

                  - code [ref=f84e1276]: isize::MAX

                - heading "Time complexity" [level=5] [ref=f84e1282]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1283]:
                  - text: Takes amortized
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1284]: O
                  - text: (1) time. If the vector’s length would exceed its capacity after the push,
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1285]: O
                  - text: (
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1286]: capacity
                  - text: ) time is taken to copy the vector’s elements to a larger allocation. This expensive operation is offset by the
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1287]: capacity
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1288]: O
                  - text: (1) insertions it allows.

              - generic [ref=f84e1386]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1387]:
                  - text: Creates a
                  - code [ref=f84e1388]: Vec<T, A>
                  - text: directly from a pointer, a length, a capacity, and an allocator.
                - heading "Safety" [level=5] [ref=f84e1389]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1390]: "This is highly unsafe, due to the number of invariants that aren’t checked:"
                - list [ref=f84e1391]:
                  - listitem [ref=f84e1392]:
                    - code [ref=f84e1393]: ptr
                    - text: must be
                    - link [ref=f84e1394] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../alloc/trait.Allocator.html#currently-allocated-memory
                      - emphasis [ref=f84e1395]: currently allocated
                    - text: via the given allocator
                    - code [ref=f84e1396]: alloc
                    - text: .
                  - listitem [ref=f84e1397]:
                    - code [ref=f84e1398]: T
                    - text: needs to have the same alignment as what
                    - code [ref=f84e1399]: ptr
                    - text: was allocated with. (
                    - code [ref=f84e1400]: T
                    - text: having a less strict alignment is not sufficient, the alignment really needs to be equal to satisfy the
                    - link [ref=f84e1401] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#tymethod.dealloc
                      - code [ref=f84e1402]: dealloc
                    - text: requirement that memory must be allocated and deallocated with the same layout.)
                  - listitem [ref=f84e1403]:
                    - text: The size of
                    - code [ref=f84e1404]: T
                    - text: times the
                    - code [ref=f84e1405]: capacity
                    - text: (i.e. the allocated size in bytes) needs to be the same size as the pointer was allocated with. (Because similar to alignment,
                    - link [ref=f84e1406] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#tymethod.dealloc
                      - code [ref=f84e1407]: dealloc
                    - text: must be called with the same layout
                    - code [ref=f84e1408]: size
                    - text: .)
                  - listitem [ref=f84e1409]:
                    - code [ref=f84e1410]: length
                    - text: needs to be less than or equal to
                    - code [ref=f84e1411]: capacity
                    - text: .
                  - listitem [ref=f84e1412]:
                    - text: The first
                    - code [ref=f84e1413]: length
                    - text: values must be properly initialized values of type
                    - code [ref=f84e1414]: T
                    - text: .
                  - listitem [ref=f84e1415]:
                    - code [ref=f84e1416]: capacity
                    - text: needs to
                    - link [ref=f84e1417] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../alloc/trait.Allocator.html#memory-fitting
                      - emphasis [ref=f84e1418]: fit
                    - text: the layout size that the pointer was allocated with.
                  - listitem [ref=f84e1419]:
                    - text: The allocated size in bytes must be no larger than
                    - code [ref=f84e1420]: isize::MAX
                    - text: . See the safety documentation of
                    - link [ref=f84e1421] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../primitive.pointer.html#method.offset
                      - code [ref=f84e1422]: pointer::offset
                    - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1423]:
                  - text: These requirements are always upheld by any
                  - code [ref=f84e1424]: ptr
                  - text: that has been allocated via
                  - code [ref=f84e1425]: Vec<T, A>
                  - text: . Other allocation sources are allowed if the invariants are upheld.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1426]:
                  - text: Violating these may cause problems like corrupting the allocator’s internal data structures. For example it is
                  - strong [ref=f84e1427]: not
                  - text: safe to build a
                  - code [ref=f84e1428]: Vec<u8>
                  - text: from a pointer to a C
                  - code [ref=f84e1429]: char
                  - text: array with length
                  - code [ref=f84e1430]: size_t
                  - text: . It’s also not safe to build one from a
                  - code [ref=f84e1431]: Vec<u16>
                  - text: and its length, because the allocator cares about the alignment, and these two types have different alignments. The buffer was allocated with alignment 2 (for
                  - code [ref=f84e1432]: u16
                  - text: ), but after turning it into a
                  - code [ref=f84e1433]: Vec<u8>
                  - text: it’ll be deallocated with alignment 1.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1434]:
                  - text: The ownership of
                  - code [ref=f84e1435]: ptr
                  - text: is effectively transferred to the
                  - code [ref=f84e1436]: Vec<T>
                  - text: which may then deallocate, reallocate or change the contents of memory pointed to by the pointer at will. Ensure that nothing else uses the pointer after calling this function.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e1437]
                - code [ref=f84e1440]: "#![feature(allocator_api)] use std::alloc::System; use std::ptr; let mut v = Vec::with_capacity_in(3, System); v.push(1); v.push(2); v.push(3); // Deconstruct the vector into parts. let (p, len, cap, alloc) = v.into_raw_parts_with_alloc(); unsafe { // Overwrite memory with 4, 5, 6 for i in 0..len { ptr::write(p.add(i), 4 + i); } // Put everything back together into a Vec let rebuilt = Vec::from_raw_parts_in(p, len, cap, alloc.clone()); assert_eq!(rebuilt, [4, 5, 6]); }"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1441]: "Using memory that was allocated elsewhere:"
                - code [ref=f84e1444]: "#![feature(allocator_api)] use std::alloc::{AllocError, Allocator, Global, Layout}; fn main() { let layout = Layout::array::<u32>(16).expect(\"overflow cannot happen\"); let vec = unsafe { let mem = match Global.allocate(layout) { Ok(mem) => mem.cast::<u32>().as_ptr(), Err(AllocError) => return, }; mem.write(1_000_000); Vec::from_raw_parts_in(mem, 1, 16, Global) }; assert_eq!(vec, &[1_000_000]); assert_eq!(vec.capacity(), 16); }"

                  - code [ref=f84e1543]: Vec

              - generic [ref=f84e1590]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1591]: Returns the total number of elements the vector can hold without reallocating.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e1592]

            - group [ref=f84e1600]:
              - generic [ref=f84e1601]:
                - generic [ref=f84e1602]:
                  - generic [ref=f84e1603]:
                    - text: 1.0.0 ·
                    - link "Source" [ref=f84e1604] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: ../../src/alloc/vec/mod.rs.html#1460
                  - heading [level=4] [ref=f84e1605]:
                    - text: pub fn
                    - link "reserve" [ref=f84e1606] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#method.reserve"

                    - link "usize" [ref=f84e1607] [cursor=pointer]:

              - generic [ref=f84e1608]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1609]:
                  - text: Reserves capacity for at least
                  - code [ref=f84e1610]: additional
                  - text: more elements to be inserted in the given
                  - code [ref=f84e1611]: Vec<T>
                  - text: . The collection may reserve more space to speculatively avoid frequent reallocations. After calling
                  - code [ref=f84e1612]: reserve
                  - text: ", capacity will be greater than or equal to"
                  - code [ref=f84e1613]: self.len() + additional
                  - text: . Does nothing if capacity is already sufficient.
                - heading "Panics" [level=5] [ref=f84e1614]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1615]:
                  - text: Panics if the new capacity exceeds
                  - code [ref=f84e1616]: isize::MAX
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e1617]: bytes
                  - text: .
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e1618]

                  - code [ref=f84e1861]: len

                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.drain
                    - code [ref=f84e1864]: drain
                  - text: method can emulate
                  - code [ref=f84e1865]: truncate
                  - text: ", but causes the excess elements to be returned instead of dropped."
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1866]: Note that this method has no effect on the allocated capacity of the vector.

              - generic [ref=f84e1924]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1925]: Returns a raw pointer to the vector’s buffer, or a dangling raw pointer valid for zero sized reads if the vector didn’t allocate.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1926]: The caller must ensure that the vector outlives the pointer this function returns, or else it will end up dangling. Modifying the vector may cause its buffer to be reallocated, which would also make any pointers to it invalid.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1927]:
                  - text: The caller must also ensure that the memory the pointer (non-transitively) points to is never written to (except inside an
                  - code [ref=f84e1928]: UnsafeCell
                  - text: ) using this pointer or any pointer derived from it. If you need to mutate the contents of the slice, use
                  - link [ref=f84e1929] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.as_mut_ptr
                    - code [ref=f84e1930]: as_mut_ptr
                  - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1931]:
                  - text: This method guarantees that for the purpose of the aliasing model, this method does not materialize a reference to the underlying slice, and thus the returned pointer will remain valid when mixed with other calls to
                  - link [ref=f84e1932] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.as_ptr
                    - code [ref=f84e1933]: as_ptr
                  - text: ","
                  - link [ref=f84e1934] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.as_mut_ptr
                    - code [ref=f84e1935]: as_mut_ptr
                  - text: ", and"
                  - link [ref=f84e1936] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.as_non_null
                    - code [ref=f84e1937]: as_non_null
                  - text: . Note that calling other methods that materialize mutable references to the slice, or mutable references to specific elements you are planning on accessing through this pointer, as well as writing to those elements, may still invalidate this pointer. See the second example below for how this guarantee can be used.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e1938]
                - code [ref=f84e1941]: "let x = vec![1, 2, 4]; let x_ptr = x.as_ptr(); unsafe { for i in 0..x.len() { assert_eq!(*x_ptr.add(i), 1 << i); } }"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1942]: "Due to the aliasing guarantee, the following code is legal:"
                - code [ref=f84e1945]: "unsafe { let mut v = vec![0, 1, 2]; let ptr1 = v.as_ptr(); let _ = ptr1.read(); let ptr2 = v.as_mut_ptr().offset(2); ptr2.write(2); // Notably, the write to `ptr2` did *not* invalidate `ptr1` // because it mutated a different element: let _ = ptr1.read(); }"

              - generic [ref=f84e1954]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1955]: Returns a raw mutable pointer to the vector’s buffer, or a dangling raw pointer valid for zero sized reads if the vector didn’t allocate.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1956]: The caller must ensure that the vector outlives the pointer this function returns, or else it will end up dangling. Modifying the vector may cause its buffer to be reallocated, which would also make any pointers to it invalid.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1957]:
                  - text: This method guarantees that for the purpose of the aliasing model, this method does not materialize a reference to the underlying slice, and thus the returned pointer will remain valid when mixed with other calls to
                  - link [ref=f84e1958] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.as_ptr
                    - code [ref=f84e1959]: as_ptr
                  - text: ","
                  - link [ref=f84e1960] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.as_mut_ptr
                    - code [ref=f84e1961]: as_mut_ptr
                  - text: ", and"
                  - link [ref=f84e1962] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.as_non_null
                    - code [ref=f84e1963]: as_non_null
                  - text: . Note that calling other methods that materialize references to the slice, or references to specific elements you are planning on accessing through this pointer, may still invalidate this pointer. See the second example below for how this guarantee can be used.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1964]:
                  - text: The method also guarantees that, as long as
                  - code [ref=f84e1965]: T
                  - text: is not zero-sized and the capacity is nonzero, the pointer may be passed into
                  - link [ref=f84e1966] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#tymethod.dealloc
                    - code [ref=f84e1967]: dealloc
                  - text: with a layout of
                  - code [ref=f84e1968]: Layout::array::<T>(capacity)
                  - text: in order to deallocate the backing memory. If this is done, be careful not to run the destructor of the
                  - code [ref=f84e1969]: Vec
                  - text: ", as dropping it will result in double-frees. Wrapping the"
                  - code [ref=f84e1970]: Vec
                  - text: in a
                  - link [ref=f84e1971] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../mem/struct.ManuallyDrop.html
                    - code [ref=f84e1972]: ManuallyDrop
                  - text: is the typical way to achieve this.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e1973]
                - code [ref=f84e1976]: "// Allocate vector big enough for 4 elements. let size = 4; let mut x: Vec<i32> = Vec::with_capacity(size); let x_ptr = x.as_mut_ptr(); // Initialize elements via raw pointer writes, then set length. unsafe { for i in 0..size { *x_ptr.add(i) = i as i32; } x.set_len(size); } assert_eq!(&*x, &[0, 1, 2, 3]);"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1977]: "Due to the aliasing guarantee, the following code is legal:"
                - code [ref=f84e1980]: "unsafe { let mut v = vec![0]; let ptr1 = v.as_mut_ptr(); ptr1.write(1); let ptr2 = v.as_mut_ptr(); ptr2.write(2); // Notably, the write to `ptr2` did *not* invalidate `ptr1`: ptr1.write(3); }"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e1981]:
                  - text: Deallocating a vector using
                  - link [ref=f84e1982] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../boxed/struct.Box.html

                  - text: (which uses
                  - link [ref=f84e1984] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../alloc/trait.GlobalAlloc.html#tymethod.dealloc

                  - text: "internally):"
                - code [ref=f84e1988]: "use std::mem::{ManuallyDrop, MaybeUninit}; let mut v = ManuallyDrop::new(vec![0, 1, 2]); let ptr = v.as_mut_ptr(); let capacity = v.capacity(); let slice_ptr: *mut [MaybeUninit<i32>] = std::ptr::slice_from_raw_parts_mut(ptr.cast(), capacity); drop(unsafe { Box::from_raw(slice_ptr) });"

              - generic [ref=f84e2045]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2046]:
                  - text: Forces the length of the vector to
                  - code [ref=f84e2047]: new_len
                  - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2048]:
                  - text: This is a low-level operation that maintains none of the normal invariants of the type. Normally changing the length of a vector is done using one of the safe operations instead, such as
                  - link [ref=f84e2049] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.truncate
                    - code [ref=f84e2050]: truncate
                  - text: ","
                  - link [ref=f84e2051] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.resize
                    - code [ref=f84e2052]: resize
                  - text: ","
                  - link [ref=f84e2053] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../iter/trait.Extend.html#tymethod.extend
                    - code [ref=f84e2054]: extend
                  - text: ", or"
                  - link [ref=f84e2055] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.clear
                    - code [ref=f84e2056]: clear
                  - text: .
                - heading "Safety" [level=5] [ref=f84e2057]
                - list [ref=f84e2058]:
                  - listitem [ref=f84e2059]:
                    - code [ref=f84e2060]: new_len
                    - text: must be less than or equal to
                    - link [ref=f84e2061] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.capacity
                      - code [ref=f84e2062]: capacity()
                    - text: .
                  - listitem [ref=f84e2063]:
                    - text: The elements at
                    - code [ref=f84e2064]: old_len..new_len
                    - text: must be initialized.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e2065]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2066]:
                  - text: See
                  - link [ref=f84e2067] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.spare_capacity_mut
                    - code [ref=f84e2068]: spare_capacity_mut()
                  - text: for an example with safe initialization of capacity elements and use of this method.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2069]:
                  - code [ref=f84e2070]: set_len()
                  - text: "can be useful for situations in which the vector is serving as a buffer for other code, particularly over FFI:"
                - code [ref=f84e2073]: "pub fn get_dictionary(&self) -> Option<Vec<u8>> { // Per the FFI method's docs, \"32768 bytes is always enough\". let mut dict = Vec::with_capacity(32_768); let mut dict_length = 0; // SAFETY: When `deflateGetDictionary` returns `Z_OK`, it holds that: // 1. `dict_length` elements were initialized. // 2. `dict_length` <= the capacity (32_768) // which makes `set_len` safe to call. unsafe { // Make the FFI call... let r = deflateGetDictionary(self.strm, dict.as_mut_ptr(), &mut dict_length); if r == Z_OK { // ...and update the length to what was initialized. dict.set_len(dict_length); Some(dict) } else { None } } }"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2074]:
                  - text: While the following example is sound, there is a memory leak since the inner vectors were not freed prior to the
                  - code [ref=f84e2075]: set_len
                  - text: "call:"
                - code [ref=f84e2078]: "let mut vec = vec![vec![1, 0, 0], vec![0, 1, 0], vec![0, 0, 1]]; // SAFETY: // 1. `old_len..0` is empty so no elements need to be initialized. // 2. `0 <= capacity` always holds whatever `capacity` is. unsafe { vec.set_len(0); }"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2079]:
                  - text: Normally, here, one would use
                  - link [ref=f84e2080] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.clear
                    - code [ref=f84e2081]: clear
                  - text: instead to correctly drop the contents and thus not leak memory.

                - paragraph [ref=f84e2092]: The removed element is replaced by the last element of the vector.

                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.remove

                  - text: instead.

                  - text: within the vector, shifting all elements after it to the left.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2162]:
                  - text: "Note: Because this shifts over the remaining elements, it has a worst-case performance of"
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e2163]: O
                  - text: (
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e2164]: "n"
                  - text: ). If you don’t need the order of elements to be preserved, use
                  - link [ref=f84e2165] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.swap_remove
                    - code [ref=f84e2166]: swap_remove
                  - text: instead. If you’d like to remove elements from the beginning of the
                  - code [ref=f84e2167]: Vec

                    - /url: ../collections/struct.VecDeque.html#method.pop_front

              - generic [ref=f84e2216]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2217]: Retains only the elements specified by the predicate.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2218]:

                  - code [ref=f84e2219]: e
                  - text: for which
                  - code [ref=f84e2220]: f(&e)
                  - text: returns
                  - code [ref=f84e2221]: "false"
                  - text: . This method operates in place, visiting each element exactly once in the original order, and preserves the order of the retained elements.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e2222]
                - code [ref=f84e2225]: let mut vec = vec![1, 2, 3, 4]; vec.retain(|&x| x % 2 == 0); assert_eq!(vec, [2, 4]);
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2226]: Because the elements are visited exactly once in the original order, external state may be used to decide which elements to keep.
                - code [ref=f84e2229]: let mut vec = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; let keep = [false, true, true, false, true]; let mut iter = keep.iter(); vec.retain(|_| *iter.next().unwrap()); assert_eq!(vec, [2, 3, 5]);

              - generic [ref=f84e2281]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2282]: Removes all but the first of consecutive elements in the vector that are “equal” according to the given predicate function.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2283]:
                  - text: The predicate
                  - code [ref=f84e2284]: same_bucket(x, p)
                  - text: is passed references to two elements. If it returns
                  - code [ref=f84e2285]: "true"
                  - text: ", the element"
                  - code [ref=f84e2286]: x
                  - text: is removed from the vector.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2287]:
                  - text: The element
                  - code [ref=f84e2288]: p
                  - text: occurs
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e2289]: before
                  - code [ref=f84e2290]: x
                  - text: in the vector (
                  - code [ref=f84e2291]: "[.., p, .., x, ..]"
                  - text: ), so
                  - code [ref=f84e2292]: same_bucket(x, p)
                  - text: is receiving them in reversed order (unlike
                  - link [ref=f84e2293] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../primitive.slice.html#method.windows
                    - code [ref=f84e2294]: windows
                  - text: ).
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2295]: If the vector is sorted, this removes all duplicates. For more complicated predicates however, the order (ascending vs. descending) can matter.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e2296]
                - code [ref=f84e2299]: let mut vec = vec!["foo", "bar", "Bar", "baz", "bar"]; vec.dedup_by(|x, p| x.eq_ignore_ascii_case(p)); assert_eq!(vec, ["foo", "bar", "baz", "bar"]);
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2300]:
                  - text: Both references passed to
                  - code [ref=f84e2301]: same_bucket
                  - text: are mutable. This allows merging elements by mutating
                  - code [ref=f84e2302]: p
                  - text: and returning
                  - code [ref=f84e2303]: "true"
                  - text: ":"
                - code [ref=f84e2306]: "let mut ranges = vec![1..2, 2..4, 2..5, 8..9]; // Sort ranges by start, and if equal, by end (lexicographically) // Sorting in reverse instead (`x.start.cmp(&p.start)...`) would later fail ranges.sort_unstable_by(|p, x| p.start.cmp(&x.start).then(p.end.cmp(&x.end))); // Merge touching (`1..2` and `2..4`) and then overlapping (`1..4` and `2..5`) ranges ranges.dedup_by(|x, p| { if p.end >= x.start { p.end = p.end.max(x.end); true } else { false } }); assert_eq!(ranges, [1..5, 8..9]);"
            - group [ref=f84e2307]:

              - generic [ref=f84e2320]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2321]: Appends an element and returns a reference to it if there is sufficient spare capacity, otherwise an error is returned with the element.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2322]:
                  - text: Unlike
                  - link [ref=f84e2323] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.push
                    - code [ref=f84e2324]: push
                  - text: this method will not reallocate when there’s insufficient capacity. The caller should use
                  - link [ref=f84e2325] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.reserve
                    - code [ref=f84e2326]: reserve
                  - text: or
                  - link [ref=f84e2327] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.try_reserve
                    - code [ref=f84e2328]: try_reserve
                  - text: to ensure that there is enough capacity.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e2329]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2330]:
                  - text: A manual, panic-free alternative to
                  - link [ref=f84e2331] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../iter/trait.FromIterator.html
                    - code [ref=f84e2332]: FromIterator
                  - text: ":"
                - code [ref=f84e2335]: "#![feature(vec_push_within_capacity)] use std::collections::TryReserveError; fn from_iter_fallible<T>(iter: impl Iterator<Item=T>) -> Result<Vec<T>, TryReserveError> { let mut vec = Vec::new(); for value in iter { if let Err(value) = vec.push_within_capacity(value) { vec.try_reserve(1)?; // this cannot fail, the previous line either returned or added at least 1 free slot let _ = vec.push_within_capacity(value); } } Ok(vec) } assert_eq!(from_iter_fallible(0..100), Ok(Vec::from_iter(0..100)));"
                - heading "Time complexity" [level=5] [ref=f84e2336]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2337]:
                  - text: Takes
                  - emphasis [ref=f84e2338]: O
                  - text: (1) time.

              - generic [ref=f84e2435]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2436]: Removes the subslice indicated by the given range from the vector, returning a double-ended iterator over the removed subslice.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2437]: If the iterator is dropped before being fully consumed, it drops the remaining removed elements.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2438]: The returned iterator keeps a mutable borrow on the vector to optimize its implementation.
                - heading "Panics" [level=5] [ref=f84e2439]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2440]:
                  - text: Panics if the range has
                  - code [ref=f84e2441]: start_bound > end_bound
                  - text: ", or, if the range is bounded on either end and past the length of the vector."
                - heading "Leaking" [level=5] [ref=f84e2442]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2443]:
                  - text: If the returned iterator goes out of scope without being dropped (due to
                  - link [ref=f84e2444] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: ../mem/fn.forget.html
                    - code [ref=f84e2445]: mem::forget
                  - text: ", for example), the vector may have lost and leaked elements arbitrarily, including elements outside the range."
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e2446]
                - code [ref=f84e2449]: "let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3]; let u: Vec<_> = v.drain(1..).collect(); assert_eq!(v, &[1]); assert_eq!(u, &[2, 3]); // A full range clears the vector, like `clear()` does v.drain(..); assert_eq!(v, &[]);"

                  - code [ref=f84e2541]: len

                  - code [ref=f84e2547]: f

                  - code [ref=f84e2548]: f
                  - text: will end up in the
                  - code [ref=f84e2549]: Vec

              - generic [ref=f84e2699]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2700]:
                  - text: This clears out this
                  - code [ref=f84e2701]: Vec
                  - text: and recycles the allocation into a new
                  - code [ref=f84e2702]: Vec
                  - text: . The item type of the resulting
                  - code [ref=f84e2703]: Vec
                  - text: needs to have the same size and alignment as the item type of the original
                  - code [ref=f84e2704]: Vec

              - generic [ref=f84e2913]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2914]:
                  - text: Creates a splicing iterator that replaces the specified range in the vector with the given
                  - code [ref=f84e2915]: replace_with
                  - text: iterator and yields the removed items.
                  - code [ref=f84e2916]: replace_with
                  - text: does not need to be the same length as
                  - code [ref=f84e2917]: range
                  - text: .
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2918]:
                  - code [ref=f84e2919]: range
                  - text: is removed even if the
                  - code [ref=f84e2920]: Splice
                  - text: iterator is not consumed before it is dropped.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2921]:
                  - text: It is unspecified how many elements are removed from the vector if the
                  - code [ref=f84e2922]: Splice
                  - text: value is leaked.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2923]:
                  - text: The input iterator
                  - code [ref=f84e2924]: replace_with
                  - text: is only consumed when the
                  - code [ref=f84e2925]: Splice
                  - text: value is dropped.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2926]: "This is optimal if:"
                - list [ref=f84e2927]:
                  - listitem [ref=f84e2928]:
                    - text: The tail (elements in the vector after
                    - code [ref=f84e2929]: range
                    - text: ) is empty,
                  - listitem [ref=f84e2930]:
                    - text: or
                    - code [ref=f84e2931]: replace_with
                    - text: yields fewer or equal elements than
                    - code [ref=f84e2932]: range
                    - text: ’s length
                  - listitem [ref=f84e2933]:
                    - text: or the lower bound of its
                    - code [ref=f84e2934]: size_hint()
                    - text: is exact.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2935]: Otherwise, a temporary vector is allocated and the tail is moved twice.
                - heading "Panics" [level=5] [ref=f84e2936]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2937]:
                  - text: Panics if the range has
                  - code [ref=f84e2938]: start_bound > end_bound
                  - text: ", or, if the range is bounded on either end and past the length of the vector."
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e2939]
                - code [ref=f84e2942]: "let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3, 4]; let new = [7, 8, 9]; let u: Vec<_> = v.splice(1..3, new).collect(); assert_eq!(v, [1, 7, 8, 9, 4]); assert_eq!(u, [2, 3]);"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2943]:
                  - text: Using
                  - code [ref=f84e2944]: splice
                  - text: "to insert new items into a vector efficiently at a specific position indicated by an empty range:"
                - code [ref=f84e2947]: let mut v = vec![1, 5]; let new = [2, 3, 4]; v.splice(1..1, new); assert_eq!(v, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
            - group [ref=f84e2948]:
              - generic [ref=f84e2949]:
                - generic [ref=f84e2950]:
                  - generic [ref=f84e2951]:

                  - heading [level=4] [ref=f84e2953]:
                    - text: pub fn
                    - link "extract_if" [ref=f84e2954] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#method.extract_if"
                    - text: "<F, R>( &mut self, range: R, filter: F, ) ->"
                    - link "ExtractIf" [ref=f84e2955] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: struct.ExtractIf.html
                    - text: <'_, T, F, A>
                    - link "ⓘ" [ref=f84e2956] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#"
                    - generic [ref=f84e2957]:
                      - text: "where F:"
                      - link "FnMut" [ref=f84e2958] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: ../ops/trait.FnMut.html
                      - text: (
                      - link "&mut T" [ref=f84e2959] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: ../primitive.reference.html
                      - text: ) ->
                      - link "bool" [ref=f84e2960] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: ../primitive.bool.html
                      - text: ", R:"
                      - link "RangeBounds" [ref=f84e2961] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: ../ops/trait.RangeBounds.html
                      - text: <
                      - link "usize" [ref=f84e2962] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: ../primitive.usize.html
                      - text: ">,"
                - text: Collapse
              - generic [ref=f84e2963]:
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2964]: Creates an iterator which uses a closure to determine if an element in the range should be removed.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2965]:
                  - text: If the closure returns
                  - code [ref=f84e2966]: "true"
                  - text: ", the element is removed from the vector and yielded. If the closure returns"
                  - code [ref=f84e2967]: "false"
                  - text: ", or panics, the element remains in the vector and will not be yielded."
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2968]: Only elements that fall in the provided range are considered for extraction, but any elements after the range will still have to be moved if any element has been extracted.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2969]:
                  - text: If the returned
                  - code [ref=f84e2970]: ExtractIf
                  - text: is not exhausted, e.g. because it is dropped without iterating or the iteration short-circuits, then the remaining elements will be retained. Use
                  - code [ref=f84e2971]: extract_if().for_each(drop)
                  - text: if you do not need the returned iterator, or
                  - link [ref=f84e2972] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: struct.Vec.html#method.retain_mut
                    - code [ref=f84e2973]: retain_mut
                  - text: with a negated predicate if you also do not need to restrict the range.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2974]: "Using this method is equivalent to the following code:"
                - code [ref=f84e2977]: "let mut i = range.start; let end_items = vec.len() - range.end; while i < vec.len() - end_items { if some_predicate(&mut vec[i]) { let val = vec.remove(i); // your code here } else { i += 1; } }"
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2978]:
                  - text: But
                  - code [ref=f84e2979]: extract_if
                  - text: is easier to use.
                  - code [ref=f84e2980]: extract_if
                  - text: is also more efficient, because it can backshift the elements of the array in bulk.
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2981]: The iterator also lets you mutate the value of each element in the closure, regardless of whether you choose to keep or remove it.
                - heading "Panics" [level=5] [ref=f84e2982]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2983]:
                  - text: If
                  - code [ref=f84e2984]: range
                  - text: is out of bounds.
                - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e2985]
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2986]: "Splitting a vector into even and odd values, reusing the original vector:"
                - code [ref=f84e2989]: let mut numbers = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 15]; let evens = numbers.extract_if(.., |x| *x % 2 == 0).collect::<Vec<_>>(); let odds = numbers; assert_eq!(evens, vec![2, 4, 6, 8, 14]); assert_eq!(odds, vec![1, 3, 5, 9, 11, 13, 15]);
                - paragraph [ref=f84e2990]: "Using the range argument to only process a part of the vector:"
                - code [ref=f84e2993]: let mut items = vec![0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2]; let ones = items.extract_if(7.., |x| *x == 1).collect::<Vec<_>>(); assert_eq!(items, vec![0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 2, 2]); assert_eq!(ones.len(), 3);

            - generic [ref=f84e3444]:
              - paragraph [ref=f84e3445]: Returns a raw pointer to the slice’s buffer.
              - paragraph [ref=f84e3446]: The caller must ensure that the slice outlives the pointer this function returns, or else it will end up dangling.
              - paragraph [ref=f84e3447]:
                - text: The caller must also ensure that the memory the pointer (non-transitively) points to is never written to (except inside an
                - code [ref=f84e3448]: UnsafeCell
                - text: ) using this pointer or any pointer derived from it. If you need to mutate the contents of the slice, use
                - link [ref=f84e3449] [cursor=pointer]:
                  - /url: ../primitive.slice.html#method.as_mut_ptr
                  - code [ref=f84e3450]: as_mut_ptr
                - text: .
              - paragraph [ref=f84e3451]: Modifying the container referenced by this slice may cause its buffer to be reallocated, which would also make any pointers to it invalid.
              - heading "Examples" [level=5] [ref=f84e3452]
